# Monetization & Product Governance for a Single Global Title
## "One Game, Many Acquisition Paths"

---

## 1. The core diagnostic

Global live-service monetization fails in five recognisable ways, and all five are versions of the same mistake: treating monetization as a *feature of the game* when it is in fact a *regulated product sold into ~150 separate consumer-law jurisdictions through two platform gatekeepers*.

**A build is not a jurisdiction.** Your unit of legal exposure is the SKU-in-store-in-country, under a specific age rating, sold by a specific publisher of record, priced in a specific currency, under a specific consumer-protection code. GRAC, NPPA, PEGI, the Belgian Gaming Commission, the Kansspelautoriteit, CADE/Senacon, the FTC and forty-odd state AGs did not approve your economy design. They approved — or tolerate — a product. Any plan that treats loot-box compliance as a regional feature flag on a single global economy will discover in year two that it has shipped an unlicensed gambling product in three markets and an unfair-commercial-practice in five more.

**Disclosure is global even when regulation is local. This is the structural fact that changes everything.** The probability tables you publish for Korea are readable by a Belgian legislator, a Dutch consumer lawyer, a Brazilian prosecutor, a Japanese self-regulatory body and a US class-action firm — on the same afternoon. Player-protection advocacy is now a coordinated, well-instrumented, cross-border research function. There is no longer such a thing as a quiet local variant. **You must be defensible at the strictest *disclosed* standard, not the local legal minimum.**

**Rebuilding the economy engine is the highest-variance activity in live service, and it is almost never the source of the value.** A global economy re-platform — ripping out gacha, converting wallets, resetting price ladders — has destroyed more live-service titles than any content failure. The downside is not a bad quarter; it is whale exodus, a community revolt that becomes the regulatory exhibit, and the loss of the economy designers who understood the curve. **Economy replacement is the last thing you do, per market, one at a time.**

**Wallets and entitlements are not fungible; design capability is.** Premium currency purchased in Brazil at PIX pricing cannot be spent by an account playing in the Gulf without creating instant grey-market arbitrage, VAT exposure and refund chaos. China requires a separate publisher of record, separate data plane and separate release train. Extract global value from the **content pipeline, the live-ops calendar, the item graph and the shared models** — not from a single global ledger.

**Regulation only ratchets in one direction, and it ratchets fastest where you were most aggressive.** Every market-specific monetization mechanic you build today is a retrofit you will pay for twice: once to build, once to unwind. Design for the ratchet or refactor under legal deadline, which is the most expensive way to ship anything.

**The resolution: hold the *item graph, the competitive surface and the integrity invariants* constant; let the *acquisition path, price ladder, offer framing, event motif and payment rail* vary — on a published convergence schedule with hard caps on permanent divergence.**

The one-sentence answer to "without fragmenting the player experience": **content is global; acquisition is local.** A Belgian player and a Japanese player play the same game, in the same season, owning the same items, competing on the same ladder. They differ only in *how they bought the hat*.
